title: Discolored Tooth/Teeth

content_blocks.text: Normal tooth color varies and depends on the shade, translucency, and thickness of enamel. Translucent enamel is bluish-white, opaque enamel is gray-white.
Extrinsic—from surface accumulation of exogenous pigment.
Intrinsic—secondary to endogenous factors discoloring the underlying dentin.

Amelogenesis imperfecta and dentinogenesis imperfecta in humans are inherited conditions that have many modes of inheritance. The mode of inheritance in animals has not been studied.
Discoloration of the teeth or a tooth is extremely common in all animals.
Extrinsic staining is very common, especially bacterial stains; others are less common.
Intrinsic staining is likewise very common, especially internal and external resorption, followed by localized red blood cell destruction; the other causes are rare.

Extrinsic discoloration—bacterial stains from plaque and calculus; foods; gingival hemorrhage; dental restorative materials, medications (chlorhexidine, 8% stannous fluoride), metal.

Intrinsic discoloration—internal (trauma); external tooth resorption; localized red blood cell destruction in the tooth (trauma); systemic infections; medications (tetracycline); fluorosis; hyperbilirubinemia; amelogenesis imperfecta; dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Food debris lodged in the spaces between the teeth (diastema).
Specific metabolic enzyme decrease or absence—tyrosinemia.
Dental radiography is extremely useful in identifying internal or external resorption, restorative materials, or bacterial stain from coronal percolation.
